assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators opened a new class of quantum matter, defined by band topology and protected edge or surface states, and the quantum spin Hall effect gave it a concrete, measurable form. It is conceptually original, has reshaped how we classify electronic phases, and ties theory directly to transport and spectroscopy, which is the kind of discovery I value most.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group delivered the first transport observation in HgTe quantum wells. This is a clean theory-plus-experiment split into three. Other contributors (the HgTe quantum-well proposal, 3D topological insulators, ARPES confirmation) are not in the credited names, so some credit is left outside the slate.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent confirmations across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and many 3D materials with ARPES, and the physics is stable and widely taught. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe proposal and the 3D generalization sits partly outside the supplied names, so the prize configuration is contestable.
Strictly, practical applications remain limited, though that should not weigh against a discovery prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands with correlated insulating and superconducting phases in a simple, tunable carbon system, and launched the field of moire quantum materials. Theory predicted the magic angle and experiment found the phases, which is a prediction-confirmed-by-measurement story I find compelling. It is a genuine surprise from a material we thought we understood.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald computed the flat bands and the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated insulator and superconductivity. The three-way split is coherent. Others (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young, Santos and Kaxiras and others for early theory) complicate the picture.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups worldwide since 2018 and the field is very active, but the origin of superconductivity and the full phase diagram are still debated. Recognition is plausible but arguably a few years early.
uncertainties: Early theory credit (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto; Suarez Morell) and Cao as first author are outside the slate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductivity (LaFeAsO with doping, 2008) opened a second family of high-Tc superconductors after the cuprates, with a new multiband, magnetically proximate physics. It was an unexpected result in a class of materials with magnetic ions that had been considered hostile to superconductivity.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group made the original discovery and the single-name attribution is clear and clean. The follow-up rapid rise of Tc in related compounds by other groups is real but derivative of the original finding.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and independently reproduced within weeks and over many families (1111, 122, FeSe). The mechanism is still not fully settled, though the discovery itself is stable and 18 years old, so recognition is mature.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism is still debated, and a prize would rest on discovery rather than explanation.
Single laureate is a choice; the committee might prefer to add theory colleagues who are not on this slate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gave the first controllable, non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, capturing the Mott transition and, combined with DFT, enabling quantitative predictions for correlated materials. This is exactly the bridge between model theory and real-material spectra that I care about.
assessment.attribution: Vollhardt (with Metzner) introduced the infinite-dimension limit, and Georges and Kotliar developed the mapping onto the impurity problem and the DFT+DMFT extension. The credited trio is reasonable, though Metzner is not in the names and Rozenberg, Kotliar and Zhang also made key contributions.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: widely used for about 30 years, benchmarked against experiment and other methods, and now a standard tool. The question is whether the committee regards theory and method work as a discovery.
uncertainties: Approximate in finite dimensions; non-local extensions are still developing.
Whether a method rather than a physical discovery fits the prize criterion is uncertain; credit allocation leaves out Metzner.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics realised strong light-matter coupling with superconducting circuits and underpins readout and control of superconducting qubits. It is a clear, original quantum-behaviour-in-a-device result with major practical consequence.
assessment.attribution: Blais and colleagues (with Schoelkopf, Girvin) proposed the architecture, and Wallraff with Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. Credit is shared with Girvin and others, so a three-person split excludes some decisive figures.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many labs and now the basis of the leading quantum-computing platforms. It follows closely on the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which might be seen as overlap or as a natural continuation. Timing is plausible.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize topic may count against it.
Girvin and Devoret and others also have strong claims, which the supplied credit does not include.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance, and later giant TMR in MgO junctions, underlies spin-dependent tunnelling in magnetic sensors and MRAM. It is a solid, physically understood discovery with real use that complements the 2007 GMR prize.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki independently reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin led the MgO giant TMR work with Yuasa and Djayaprawira also central. The supplied names omit Yuasa, and theory by Butler and Mathon is also relevant.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed, with long commercial use. The risk is that the GMR prize in 2007 leaves less room, and that applications are seen as engineering.
uncertainties: Credit for MgO coherent tunnelling is split with persons outside the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultrasoft pseudopotentials and the projector augmented-wave method made accurate plane-wave DFT calculations efficient and general, and underlie much of modern computational materials physics. The impact is enormous, though it is a methodological contribution rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon.
assessment.attribution: Vanderbilt introduced ultrasoft pseudopotentials, Blöchl developed PAW, and Kresse and Joubert linked them in widely used codes (VASP). Credit is clear for the first two; Kresse's implementation role is substantial but Joubert is not listed.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and validated by reproducibility studies across codes, and recognition would be well timed. I declare an interest as a DFT practitioner and discount for it.
uncertainties: Method versus discovery: the 1998 chemistry prize and the physics prize criteria make this uncertain.
My own field proximity may bias the ranking upward.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on the magic-wavelength idea, reached fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and enabled tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. It is a clear instrument-level breakthrough with quantum-state engineering at its core.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice approach and Ye's group pushed the performance and many-body physics. The two-name configuration seems fair, though trapped-ion clock work and Hall and Hänsch (2005 prize) are related.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many labs and approaching redefinition of the second, so it is mature. This is outside my own expertise, so I defer to colleagues in atomic physics.
uncertainties: Outside my expertise; priority and relative credit versus ion clocks are uncertain.
Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes on precision spectroscopy and quantum control.
